extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants and early-career investigators (R01/R21/K/K99/F32/R15 applicants and PIs)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluative criteria for NIH grant applicants and PIs on eligibility, interactions with Program Officials (POs), Just-In-Time (JIT) procedures, paylines, start dates, institutional transfers, and regulatory approvals across common mechanisms (R01, R21, K, F32, R15, K99/R00).

rubrics_metrics.name: New investigator status when assigned as PI on existing grant
rubrics_metrics.description: If your institution assigns you to become a principal investigator (PI) on an existing grant that you did not apply for, you still qualify as new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is NIH policy (see NIAID link cited). Contact your PO to confirm, but taking over an existing R01 that you did not compete for generally does not disqualify you as a new investigator. Check IC-specific policies if uncertain, but the NIH-wide statement is that assignment to an existing award preserves new investigator status.

rubrics_metrics.name: How reviewers view being PI on an existing award (demonstrated capacity/experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Being PI on another R01 demonstrates capacity and experience, but if you have only been PI for a short time reviewers may not have publications or other evidence to judge your performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not a negative to have been appointed PI, but reviewers may lack concrete evidence of successful leadership if the appointment was recent. Consider whether the additional PI role materially strengthens your future submissions; discuss timing with mentor/PO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payline and fiscal-year mapping for applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications submitted to standard receipt dates in Feb-March, June-July, and Oct-Nov are almost always funded in the next fiscal year. Applications submitted in one calendar year are considered under the next FY.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know which FY's paylines will apply to your submission (standard receipt dates -> next FY). PARs/RFAs/PASs/NOSIs may have different timelines — check FOA. ICs sometimes include exceptional early-cycle apps in end-of-year spending, so consult PO for specific questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: JIT submission timing and protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Wait to submit JIT materials until requested by your PO or Grants Management Specialist (GMS); do not proactively submit JIT solely based on an eRA Commons/era-notify automatic email.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An eRA Commons email requesting JIT is a standard notice; respond when your PO/GMS explicitly asks. Submitting JIT early usually does not expedite review and may be unnecessary. If PO/GMS specifically requests JIT, comply promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: JIT is not required for Council approval
rubrics_metrics.description: JIT is not required for Council approval — Council assesses peer review and mission fit; awards require JIT for administrative processing but Council approval can occur without JIT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your application is marked 'pending' for Council, you may not have been asked for JIT yet; await PO/GMS directions. Prepare key JIT items in advance if you have time-sensitive approvals (IRB/IACUC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare JIT materials when regulatory approvals are needed
rubrics_metrics.description: If your application involves human subjects, animals, or other regulated activities, ensure IRB/IACUC and related approvals are prepared — these can delay award if not resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If approvals will take time, start them early so they won't hold up award processing. NIH can sometimes issue awards with bars on work until approvals are in place, but grants staff prefer approvals resolved before award. Ask PO whether specific JIT items are critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'pending' / 'award prepared' statuses and NOA timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Pending administrative review or 'award prepared' status is usually good news; there can be days to weeks between 'award prepared' and NOA issuance while IC director signs off and awards are queued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not inundate PO/GMS asking if award will be issued; if scored within payline and JIT completed, wait. If you need to plan (e.g., hiring) consider pre-award spending options with your institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-award spending rules
rubrics_metrics.description: You are allowed to spend in advance of award up to 90 days, subject to institutional policies and approval (institutional pre-spending account).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact your institution's grants/financial office to set up pre-spending; NIH does not manage institutional policies about pre-award charging. Use caution and document approvals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start date norms and fiscal-year constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical start dates depend on the receipt cycle (e.g., April 1 for some cycles; July 1 for Oct-Nov submissions), and ICs prefer not to process major changes late in the fiscal year; delaying start dates past Sept 30 is problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need to delay a start date, discuss it with your PO during JIT. ICs minimize end-of-FY actions; asking to move start dates after July 1 or near FY-end may be discouraged. Solid, compelling rationale will be required for delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delaying award or transferring award when changing institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: You can request a delay prior to NOA and/or arrange that the current institution decline to accept/start drawing funds so the award can be transferred to the new institution, but program staff must approve institutional change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell the PO and GMS as soon as possible (ideally during JIT) if you plan to move; they will need to assess the receiving institution's facilities/resources and may request institutional documentation/offers. Transfers are administrative and require coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: R15 PI eligibility regarding active NIH grants
rubrics_metrics.description: For R15: 'The PI may not be the PI of an active NIH research grant at the time of a R15 award, though he or she may be one of the Key Personnel for an active NIH grant held by another PD/PI.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can submit an R15 while you have an active R03 (or similar) but must not be PI of an active NIH research grant at the time the R15 award is issued; R03 may be terminated or ended (including NCE handling) to allow R15 award if scored and selected.

rubrics_metrics.name: F32 award timing relative to degree conferral and activation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An F32 award will generally not be issued/activated until the doctoral degree is conferred; activation requires signing Activation Notice and Payback Agreement and the award will not be active until those steps occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact your PO for institute-specific timing. Institutions can sometimes arrange exact duty date; check how long activation may be delayed (commonly months) and work with grants office.

rubrics_metrics.name: K99/R00 restrictions and institutional changes
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot hold a K99 while in a tenure-track faculty position; moving to a faculty position often requires withdrawing/renouncing the K99 or negotiating start/activation conditions with the PO and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you receive a faculty offer, discuss with your PO immediately — program staff may withdraw an application if they learn you already have a faculty offer inconsistent with K99 eligibility. For institutional moves, include new-institution info in JIT and prepare relevant documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple simultaneous submissions and SRG assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting multiple applications in the same cycle is allowed; SRG/SROs will evaluate each application on its own merits and should not punish PIs for multiple submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple apps are assigned to the same SRG, you may have different reviewers for each application; if you believe a reviewer should not see certain applications (conflict/DO NOT REVIEW), provide objective evidence to the SRO. The funding decision about multiple awards is up to the funding IC(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of SRO/assignment requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment request forms can be overridden; SROs and IRG leadership may reassign applications to ensure expertise balance and even distribution across SRGs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want clarity on why assignments were changed, contact the SRO for the IRG; they can explain expertise/volume reasons. If you have legitimate do-not-review concerns, present objective evidence to SRO.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to contact Program Official after a summary statement
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are within the payline or clearly competitive, you usually need not contact the PO about the summary statement. If you are unsure about funding chances or planning resubmission, contact the PO for advice on whether to resubmit and what to address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask PO whether to resubmit, what reviewers' main concerns were that you should address, and whether an internal rebuttal or 1-page Introduction would be useful. Do not frame the question as 'Will I be funded?'; instead ask about next steps and priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Council vs IC Director roles in funding decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Council assesses the quality of peer review and the application's fit with the IC's mission (often approving en bloc); the IC Director makes the final funding decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your PO says Council approval is likely, that is positive but not the final funding decision. Program staff may advocate internally, but final award depends on IC priorities and available funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: End-of-year discretionary funds and select pay considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: ICs set aside discretionary funds for select pay (early in the FY) and for end-of-year awards; end-of-year awards can happen when earlier planned awards required less money or were skipped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End-of-year awards may leave very little time to respond to information requests; make sure JIT and approvals are ready. Funding at year-end is possible but sometimes less predictable than select pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of current funding on final award decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Program officers may consider existing PI resources when making final funding decisions (programmatic priorities), but existing funding is not an automatic disqualifier and decisions are based on scientific merit and program need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have substantial overlapping funding (e.g., R00), discuss with PO how that might factor in; programmatic choices may favor investigators with less funding in tight budget situations, but merit remains primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to PO requests and internal rebuttals
rubrics_metrics.description: If PO requests clarifications or a rebuttal to reviewer comments, prepare concise responses; PO may use rebuttal to advocate internally or as part of revision planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a short (e.g., one-page) introduction/rebuttal addressing key summary paragraph concerns rather than replying to all individual reviewer critiques. Use PO guidance to shape resubmission strategy.
